extracted.intended_audience: law students, lawyers, policymakers, and general readers interested in U.S. administrative law and judicial review of agency action
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and doctrines governing when and how U.S. courts defer to federal agencies' interpretations of statutes and regulations (chiefly the Chevron two-step and related doctrines such as Skidmore, Auer, step zero, and the major questions doctrine). Useful for assessing the validity and weight of agency interpretations in litigation and rulemaking contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chevron two-step test
rubrics_metrics.description: A two-step analysis: first, whether Congress has directly spoken to the precise question at issue — if Congress's intent is clear, the court and agency must follow it; second, if the statute is silent or ambiguous, whether the agency's answer is based on a permissible (reasonable) construction of the statute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From the opinion: 'First, always, is the question whether Congress has directly spoken to the precise question at issue. If the intent of Congress is clear, that is the end of the matter...if the statute is silent or ambiguous ... the question for the court is whether the agency's answer is based on a permissible construction of the statute.' If the agency's interpretation is reasonable/permissible, the court must accept it. If not, the court may substitute its own interpretation. The test is deferential to agencies and aims to distinguish legal questions grounded in statutory interpretation from policy choices best left to agencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative regulations receive controlling weight unless arbitrary, capricious, or manifestly contrary
rubrics_metrics.description: Legislative regulations promulgated by an agency are 'given controlling weight unless they are arbitrary, capricious, or manifestly contrary to the statute.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle (quoted in Chevron) explains that where Congress has expressly or implicitly delegated authority to an agency to elucidate a statutory provision by regulation, courts should give such legislative regulations controlling weight, subject to the familiar standards (arbitrary-and-capricious, inconsistency with statute). The quoted language ties Chevron deference to the scope of acceptable agency rulemaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skidmore deference (weight depending on persuasiveness)
rubrics_metrics.description: The weight of an administrative interpretation depends on factors such as 'its consistency with earlier and later pronouncements' of an agency and its consistency with congressional purpose; less formal agency interpretations receive deference according to their persuasiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Skidmore (323 U.S. 134) sets a nonbinding, persuasive standard — courts consider consistency, thoroughness, reasoning, and fit with statutory purpose. The article notes Skidmore remains applicable to agency actions that do not receive Chevron deference (e.g., informal pronouncements, opinion letters).

rubrics_metrics.name: Chevron step zero / force-of-law requirement (Mead and related cases)
rubrics_metrics.description: Not all agency actions receive Chevron deference: an initial inquiry ('step zero') asks whether the agency action has the 'force of law' or otherwise is the kind of action that warrants Chevron deference; if not, Skidmore may apply instead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: United States v. Mead and subsequent cases draw a distinction: formal rulemaking (e.g., notice-and-comment rules) is likely to have force of law and receive Chevron deference, while informal agency materials (letters, guidance, no-action letters) typically do not and instead receive Skidmore-style consideration. The article references cases (Mead, Christensen, Barnhart) and scholarship (Chevron Step Zero) discussing this threshold inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Auer deference (agency interpretation of its own regulations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Deference doctrine that addresses agency interpretations of their own regulations (sometimes distinct from Chevron which addresses agency interpretations of statutes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Auer deference historically allowed agencies leeway in interpreting their own rules; Kisor v. Wilkie and related decisions have refined or limited Auer. The article notes the relationship between Auer and Chevron and that Auer concerns agency interpretive practices for existing regulations rather than statutory construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Major questions doctrine
rubrics_metrics.description: A doctrine that limits agency deference for decisions of 'deep economic and political significance' — courts will hesitate to infer that Congress intended to delegate authority on major questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article cites West Virginia v. EPA and the Roberts plurality language: extraordinary cases where the history and breadth of authority asserted and the economic and political significance provide reason to hesitate before concluding Congress meant to confer such authority. Examples include EPA rulemaking requiring costly 'outside the fence' measures and high-stakes actions like broad student loan cancellation; major questions can operate to bar Chevron deference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice-and-comment rulemaking (§ 553) as a signal of force-of-law and deference
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulations promulgated under the 'notice and comment' provisions of § 553 of the Administrative Procedure Act are likely to be treated as having the force of law and therefore more likely to receive Chevron deference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article explains that formal rulemaking under § 553 typically produces regulatory text with the force of law, which courts have been more willing to treat as eligible for Chevron deference; by contrast, agency letters and informal pronouncements lack that procedural posture and thus are less likely to receive Chevron-level weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arbitrary-and-capricious review (State Farm standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Agency rulemaking and regulations may be set aside if they are arbitrary, capricious, or otherwise inconsistent with statutory requirements (the standard from cases like Motor Vehicle Manufacturers Ass'n v. State Farm).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even where Chevron deference applies to a legislative regulation, the regulation remains subject to judicial review under APA standards — courts can invalidate agency rules that fail to show reasoned decisionmaking, are unsupported by the record, or are manifestly contrary to statute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency with agency pronouncements and congressional purpose as a factor in deference
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency interpretation's weight is affected by its consistency with earlier and later agency pronouncements and with the overall congressional purpose behind the statute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted from Skidmore and relied upon by Chevron, this guidance counsels that inconsistent shifts in agency position or interpretations that conflict with statutory aims reduce the persuasiveness (or appropriateness) of deference. The D.C. Circuit's reversal of EPA in Chevron's factual history relied in part on prior agency case law inconsistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courts' duty to interpret law when Congress has spoken
rubrics_metrics.description: If Congress has 'directly spoken to the precise question at issue' and the statutory intent is clear, the court must give effect to Congress's unambiguously expressed intent (the court's role is to say what the law is).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle is embedded in Chevron Step One and reflects the judiciary's constitutional role (Marbury v. Madison) and APA §706: judicial review includes deciding 'all relevant questions of law.' It is an explicit limit on agency deference — where Congress is clear, there is no room to defer.
